Curacao Oil Producers Hit by Ongoing Sanctions, Operations Disrupted

A sweeping round of international sanctions targeting Curacao’s oil and gas producers has thrown the island’s industry into turmoil, with operations disrupted at key sites and uncertainty clouding the sector’s immediate future.

The sanctions, imposed by a coalition of Western governments in response to Curacao’s alleged support for sanctioned third-party oil shipments, took effect early this week. Authorities have blocked fuel exports from several major terminals, including the Isla Refining Complex and the Boka Seaport Facility, operated respectively by CuroPetro NV and Antilles Energy Partners.

Industry sources confirmed Thursday that on-site activities at both sites have been sharply curtailed, with crude storage and outbound shipments halted pending further clarification. “We are in ongoing discussions with regulators and are seeking a resolution that allows for a safe and compliant resumption of activities,” said a spokesperson for CuroPetro NV.

The Curacao Oil and Gas Producers Association (COGPA) issued a statement warning that the sanctions could have “profound and immediate effects” on the island’s production and export capacity. “Our members collectively process and ship over 120,000 barrels of crude and refined product daily. Any prolonged disruption will severely impact operational continuity and market commitments,” said COGPA President Willem de Haan.

Union representatives also voiced concern for the workforce. “Hundreds of jobs are at risk if the terminals remain blocked,” said Maritza Romero, chair of the Oil Workers’ Union of Curacao. “We call on all parties to find a solution that ensures both compliance and job security.”

Analysts noted that the sanctions-induced standoff comes at a time when Curacao’s oil producers were ramping up output in response to regional demand. “The timing couldn’t be worse for local operators, who have invested heavily in upgrading facilities after years of underutilization,” commented Rafael Smit, an independent energy analyst based in Willemstad.

As of Friday, vessels remained anchored offshore, awaiting clearance to load or discharge cargo. Government officials said they are “actively engaging” with international partners to seek a resolution, but stressed that compliance with international norms remains paramount.

For now, the oil and gas sector on Curacao faces a tense wait, with the industry’s future hanging in the balance as sanctions continue to bite.
